design_detail: Narrative overview (published in Addiction under the heading Overview) written on behalf of the UK Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (ISCD) to update the 2004 report of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. It surveys acute and chronic physical, psychological, dependence-related and social harms of non-medical ketamine use under the nine harm categories of the rational scale of Nutt et al. (2007), with short sections on medical use, prevalence and the UK legal position. A keyword search of four databases (initially to September 2010) and a four-level evidence hierarchy are described, but no search strings, criteria, study counts, appraisal, pooling or harm scores are reported. One figure (UK deaths with ketamine mentioned, 1999–2008) and 105 references, among them case reports, letters, books, government and magazine surveys, and ten papers by one or both authors.
can_establish: Which harms of non-medical ketamine use the authors, writing for the ISCD, judged established, likely or unstudied as of about 2010–2011, organized under the nine categories of the rational harm scale, with second-hand figures and pointers to the primary studies.
cannot_establish: How common or how large any harm is, or whether ketamine causes it (selection is not reproducible, the cited evidence is neither appraised nor pooled, and most of it is case series, cross-sectional comparisons and the authors' own small groups), nor any pharmacokinetic or acute-toxicity figure that it states without a source or extrapolates from rodents.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The human evidence summarized comes from emergency-department series (London, 116 presentations; Hong Kong, 233), urology case series (9, 17 and 59 patients), the authors' own UK samples of people who use ketamine (an interview study of 90; groups of 30 using daily or frequently, and people abstinent at least a year), healthy-volunteer laboratory studies, small depression trials, national death and poisons data, surveys, and preclinical studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are described as pre-specified but are not reported. Evidence levels 3 (case reports and case series) and 4 (preclinical data) were admitted because research on ketamine was limited (p. 29).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Where given: Hong Kong emergency presentations, average age 22 years, two-thirds male (p. 30); a 16-year-old with cystitis during medical use (p. 31); young people with dilated bile ducts (p. 31).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. In the cited 1-year longitudinal study, 2 of 30 participants who used ketamine frequently died before follow-up (p. 30); attrition is not reported for any other cited study.
sample.selection_effects: Studies were chosen by the authors without reported criteria. The bladder, kidney and bile-duct evidence is from clinic case series without denominators; the evidence on cognition, psychotic-like symptoms, depression, dependence and tolerance is mostly from the authors' own volunteer samples; prevalence figures come from different surveys (the 2001 and 2009 clubber figures are from two different samples, the second published in a magazine). Sources outside the stated databases (books, a one-page practitioner article, letters, government and magazine surveys, sweeps of online drug forums) were included.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies, and rarely described: mostly self-reported frequency of use in categories defined by each source (p. 29); hair ketamine concentrations in the authors' longitudinal study (p. 33); post-mortem toxicology mentions (p. 30); administered doses in the laboratory and treatment studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as summarized: Zarate et al. (2006), 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes in treatment-resistant depression (p. 32); Aan het Rot et al. (2010), six infusions on days 0, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 12 (p. 32); Morgan et al. (2004), 0.4 or 0.8 mg/kg or placebo by intravenous infusion over 80 minutes in healthy ketamine-naive volunteers (p. 33); Lofwall et al. (2006), intramuscular ketamine in healthy adults (doses not given; p. 34, ref. 96); mice, daily injections of 5 mg/kg for 2 or 4 weeks (p. 32); rats, about five repeated doses (p. 32). Amounts used by people in the observational studies are not given; the frequency groups are daily or near-daily, frequent, infrequent (more than once a month and fewer than 3 times a week) and former use.
exposure.polysubstance: Mentioned for acute harms only: in most UK deaths with ketamine mentioned, other psychotropic drugs were mentioned too, and 11% of the London emergency presentations involved ketamine alone (p. 30). The comparison groups in the authors' studies were polydrug controls who did not use ketamine (p. 32). Other drug use is not discussed as an explanation for the urological, cognitive, psychiatric or neurological findings.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not stated for the cited studies, except a group of 30 people abstinent at least a year (p. 32) and the ex-use group of the longitudinal study (p. 31).

comparison.controls: Placebo in the laboratory and depression studies; infrequent-use, ex-use and polydrug control groups in the authors' studies; none in the urological, renal and bile-duct case series or in the death and poisons data.
comparison.matching: Not described for any cited study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measures in any cited human study of chronic harm. The review itself reports that the frequent or daily-use group of its longitudinal study had spent fewer years in education and that the subcultures concerned may differ in achievement irrespective of ketamine (p. 34), but does not consider this when it attributes memory deficits to ketamine (p. 32).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Polydrug controls who did not use ketamine in the authors' studies (p. 32); not described for other studies.

outcomes.instruments: Named only in part. Beck Depression Inventory (self-rated depressive symptoms, over 1 year; p. 31). Unnamed measures of delusions, dissociation, schizotypy and 'basic symptoms' (p. 32). Memory and executive function described by domain only (working, episodic, short- and long-term memory; visual recognition; spatial working memory; planning), with no test named (p. 32). Ratings of liking the drug and wanting more, taken during an 80-minute infusion (p. 33). Hair ketamine concentration (p. 33). Cystoscopy, CT, biopsy histology and urodynamics; serum creatinine; liver function tests; CT of the bile ducts (p. 31). PET D1 receptor binding and diffusion tensor imaging (fractional anisotropy) (p. 32). Post-mortem toxicology mentions, TOXBASE look-ups and emergency presentations (p. 30).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed. Impairment and symptom scores are not related to norms or clinical cut-offs, except that the rise in depression scores is said to be below clinical levels (p. 32).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is organized under the nine categories of the rational scale without scores or thresholds. Frequency labels follow each source and are mostly undefined in frequency, dose or duration (p. 29). The review moves between acute effects during or shortly after a single dose in healthy volunteers (transient psychotic-like symptoms, memory impairment, liking), effects in patients (people with schizophrenia; depression trials) and findings in people who use ketamine frequently (memory deficits, subclinical psychotic-like symptoms, depression scores) whose timing relative to last use is not stated; this card keeps the three apart.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for any cited study. The review does not describe randomization, counterbalancing or blinding for the placebo-controlled laboratory study it summarizes (Morgan et al., 2004, p. 33).

analysis.effect_sizes: None: no effect size, interval or test statistic is given for any harm. Figures are counts and percentages from the cited studies (key findings), for example 12 of 18 treated patients with a 50% reduction in depression measures against none of 14 given placebo (p. 32), 28 of 30 people using daily who had failed to stop (p. 33), urinary symptoms in 30% of 90 people interviewed and hydronephrosis in 30 of 59 patients (p. 31).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection with no list of included studies. The human evidence for chronic cognitive, psychiatric and dependence-related harms comes almost entirely from the authors' own studies; the pharmacokinetic and cardiac paragraphs carry no pharmacological reference; several citations do not match the sentences they support (reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable. Where sample sizes are given, the cited human studies are small: case series of 9 to 59, groups of 30, interviews with 90 or 100 people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized second-hand: ulcerative cystitis described in clinic case series (9, 17 and 59 patients), the first two of people described as dependent on ketamine, with hydronephrosis in half of the 59 and urinary symptoms reported by 30% of 90 people interviewed, without a population denominator; dilated bile ducts with abnormal liver function in six patients from three case reports; memory deficits in people using frequently, from the authors' cross-sectional studies and one 1-year longitudinal study, not found with infrequent use or in 30 people said to have been abstinent for a year (a duration that does not fit the primary report; reporting issue 16); higher subclinical delusion, dissociation and schizotypy scores with more frequent use, without evidence of clinical psychosis; depression scores rising over a year in the daily-use and ex-use groups, below clinical levels and unrelated to changes in use; concern about addiction, failed attempts to stop and craving in small groups; few adverse outcomes after large doses in medical settings; and UK deaths with ketamine mentioned rising from 2 to 22 a year between 1999 and 2008, mostly alongside other drugs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract says the literature was “systematically searched” (p. 27), but the methods give no strings, criteria, counts or appraisal and the cited evidence includes books, a magazine survey, letters and forum sweeps (p. 29): this is a narrative review. (2) The abstract concludes that neurocognitive impairment in frequent use “can impact negatively upon achievement in education and at work” and compounds addiction problems (p. 27), while the body states that there are no data on how ketamine dependence affects achievement and that the groups concerned may differ in achievement irrespective of ketamine (p. 34). (3) The body says that in a longitudinal, observational study frequent use “caused” memory impairments (p. 32), citing the wrong reference, and does not mention that the frequent-use group of the same study had fewer years of education (p. 34). (4) The abstract's neurological abnormalities that may underpin the cognitive effects (p. 27) rest on one PET and one DTI study, and the body says the white-matter changes may not be specific to ketamine (p. 32). (5) The discussion's statement that cystitis also occurs outside frequent use (p. 34) rests on a single case report during medical use (p. 31). (6) Tolerance is called “convincingly demonstrated” (p. 33) on the strength of animal studies from 1967 and 1976 and, by its title, a case report of one infant. (7) The statement that no adverse outcomes are reported after marked overdose in medical settings (p. 29) cites a report of a death. (8) The prevention and harm-reduction recommendations (pp. 27, 30, 35) are not evaluated in any cited study, and the dismissal of a forum explanation for abdominal pain as incorrect (p. 31) rests on case reports that do not test it. Against this, the body is frank about what is unknown: the incidence of dependence, a withdrawal syndrome, the mechanism of cystitis, a link with psychotic disorder, effects in pregnancy and effects on achievement.

timeline.event: Krystal et al.: single subanaesthetic doses in healthy volunteers produce transient psychotic-like symptoms; the review's example (ref. 50)

Vollenweider et al.: [18F]FDG PET study of the ketamine model of psychosis, cited by this review (ref. 69) among PET studies of striatal dopamine release although, by its title, it measured glucose metabolism

Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs technical committee report on ketamine (Nutt and King, ref. 21), the review this overview updates; the source of its statement that ketamine is not associated with violence.

Shahani et al.: first case series of ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis, 9 patients (ref. 38; on the project's Tier A list, not yet appraised). Nutt et al.: the rational harm scale used as this review's framework (ref. 22).

Chu et al.: 59 patients with lower urinary tract damage (ref. 42; Tier A). Schifano et al.: UK deaths associated with ketamine 1993–2006, the published source of Figure 1 (ref. 105; Tier A). Muetzelfeldt et al.: interviews with 90 people who use ketamine, from the authors' group (ref. 35; Tier B).
Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran: frequent, infrequent and former use compared with polydrug and non-using controls (ref. 11; Tier A).

Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran: 1-year longitudinal study, the source of the memory, depression, schizotypy, hair-analysis, education and two-deaths findings (ref. 31; Tier A, with a published erratum listed in the project's DOI list). Liao et al.: diffusion tensor imaging of frontal white matter (ref. 63; Tier B).
This review (online 2011). Winstock et al.: prevalence and natural history of urinary symptoms in people who use ketamine recreationally (Tier A; not cited by this review; not yet appraised).
Corkery et al. (deaths in England 1997–2019) and Darke et al. (circumstances of ketamine-related deaths), both on the Tier A list and not yet appraised.
Chan et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-associated uropathy (Tier A; not yet appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The review maps the harm evidence available to about 2010–2011: bladder damage known from clinic case series, chronic cognitive effects from one UK group's cross-sectional studies and a 1-year longitudinal study, dependence from interviews and case reports, acute toxicity from case reports, poisons-service and death data. Its figures are second-hand and several of its citations do not match their sentences, so claims must cite the primary studies, most of which are on the project's Tier A and B lists. Later work on the same questions is on the list (urinary symptoms, Winstock et al., 2012; deaths, Corkery et al., 2021, and Darke et al., 2021; uropathy, Chan et al., 2022) but has not been appraised, so this card says nothing about its results.

funding.funder: Acknowledgements (p. 35): “The ISCD provided a small allowance to fund the literature search.” No other funding is stated.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, Clinical Health Psychology, University College London; the review is written on behalf of the ISCD. Most of the human evidence on chronic cognitive, psychiatric, dependence-related and social harms is from the authors' own work (refs 11, 31, 35, 55, 57, 59–61, 83 and 88). People thanked for comments on the draft include authors or data providers of sources the review relies on: J. Oxley, A. Cottrell, P. Weinstock and R. Ayres (cystitis papers, refs 39, 41 and 43), D. Wood (emergency presentations, ref. 36), F. Measham (ref. 71), J. Corkery (Figure 1 data, ref. 105), R. Gable (safety ratio, ref. 23) and D. Nutt (the harm framework and the 2004 report, refs 21 and 22). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For bladder harm, a prospective cohort of people who use ketamine at known, hair-verified frequencies, with urological assessment at entry and follow-up and a polydrug comparison group, giving incidence and recovery after stopping; for cognition, a cohort assessed before or early in regular use, matched on education and other drug use and followed through continued use and cessation; and, as a synthesis, a systematic review with a reported search and appraisal for each harm.

domains.note: Four databases, a keyword approach and an initial cut-off of September 2010 are named, but no search strings, the 'pre-specified' criteria, numbers screened or included, a list of included studies or a level for any cited study are given; items up to July 2011 were added without description; many cited sources (books, a magazine survey, a one-page practitioner article, letters, forum sweeps) lie outside the stated databases. Selection cannot be reproduced.

No appraisal; the stated evidence hierarchy is not applied to any study. Case reports, letters and anecdote support general statements; a causal verb is used for an observational result; tolerance is called convincingly demonstrated from old animal studies and a single-infant case report. Some limits are named (cross-sectional studies cannot address causation; death data to be read cautiously; the safety ratio is extrapolated from rodents; white-matter changes may not be specific).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The human evidence on memory, psychotic-like symptoms, depression, dependence concerns, craving, tolerance, accidents and education comes almost entirely from the authors' own studies (refs 11, 31, 35, 55, 57, 59–61, 83, 88), partly from groups of 30 that may overlap; independent evidence in those sections is one PET and one DTI study. The handling of the authors' own longitudinal study (causal verb, wrong reference number, education difference not considered) shows the risk.

Much speculation is hedged (may, would seem, anecdotally), but some untested inferences are stated as conclusions: harm to education and work in the abstract despite the body's statement that no data exist; people using frequently 'probably already using maximal amounts'; single-dose memory effects that would profoundly affect functioning; and the classification and prevention recommendations.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm from frequent use (non-causal explanations under-represented)
domains.note: Reassuring findings are reported (few adverse outcomes after large doses in medical settings; no long-term cognitive impairment with infrequent use; no memory deficits after a year's abstinence; no evidence of clinical psychosis; depression below clinical levels; no association with violence), but other drug use, fewer years of education and the subcultural differences the review itself describes are not weighed as explanations in the cognitive, psychiatric, urological or mortality sections.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is a useful map of the harm questions as of about 2010–2011 and is frank about several unknowns (incidence of dependence, a withdrawal syndrome, the mechanism of cystitis, pregnancy, effects on achievement), but its selection is not reproducible, its evidence is not appraised, several citations do not support the sentences they are attached to, and the chronic-harm evidence rests largely on the authors' own studies. Cite it for its framework, for the questions it marks as unstudied, and as a pointer to the primary studies; take figures from the primary studies (Shahani 2007, Chu 2008, Muetzelfeldt 2008, Schifano 2008, Morgan 2009 and 2010, Zarate 2006); do not cite it for pharmacokinetic values, acute toxicity or human dopamine release. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: The review uses the nine harm categories of the rational scale of Nutt et al. (2007) as its framework: physical harms (acute, chronic, propensity for intravenous use), dependence-related harms (acute pleasure, physical dependence, psychological dependence) and social harms (intoxication, harms to the individual within society, costs to the health service). It reports a keyword search of MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Knowledge and Google Scholar against inclusion and exclusion criteria described as pre-specified but not listed, with evidence initially reviewed to September 2010, and a four-level design hierarchy (1, systematic syntheses; 2, controlled observational studies; 3, case reports and case series; 4, preclinical data), admitting levels 3 and 4 because research on ketamine was limited. Authors were contacted for clarification and new data, and online drug forums were swept for harms not in the scientific literature. No search strings, numbers screened or included, list of included studies, appraisal or harm scores are reported.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Methodology, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The review keeps each source's own labels for frequency of use, which the authors say are mostly undefined in frequency, dose or duration; 'recreational' and 'infrequent' generally mean non-dependent use confined mainly to weekends. In the depression and psychosis paragraphs, infrequent use is defined as more than once a month and fewer than 3 times a week.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › A note on terminology: frequency of ketamine use (p. 29); Depression, 1st paragraph (p. 31); Psychosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 32)
key_findings.note: The primary papers define their infrequent group as using ketamine less than four times a week but at least once a month (Morgan et al., 2009, p. 78; Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 122), not fewer than 3 times a week (reporting issue 16).

key_findings.finding: Safety ratio: Gable (ref. 23) gave ketamine a safety ratio of 25, based on a rodent oral median lethal dose (LD50) averaging about 600 mg/kg, reduced by a factor of 10 for species differences and set against an assumed oral recreational dose; a mouse study (ref. 25) suggested a much lower lethal figure of 42.9 mg/kg. The review stresses that all these estimates are extrapolated from rodent data and based on oral doses.
key_findings.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Acute physical risks › Safety ratio
key_findings.note: The review says recreational ketamine is rarely taken by mouth (p. 28), so the ratio concerns an uncommon route; see reporting issues for the inverted definition and the arithmetic. The human-equivalent lethal estimate and the assumed recreational dose are printed on the page; they are not study conditions and are not repeated on this card.

key_findings.finding: The review states that in humans ketamine has a wide margin of safety, with no adverse outcomes reported even after marked overdose in medical settings (ref. 27), and cites Green et al. (ref. 28): no adverse outcomes in nine children in emergency departments inadvertently injected with five to 100 times the intended dose. It suggests this may reflect preserved airway, cough, swallowing and gag reflexes.
key_findings.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Acute physical risks › Risk of death from an acute dose, 1st paragraph (p. 29, continuing on p. 30)
key_findings.note: The reference list gives ref. 27 as a report of a ketamine medication error resulting in death (p. 36); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 (UK post-mortem toxicology mentions of ketamine, 1999–2008; Schifano et al., ref. 105, with additional data from J. Corkery) shows, as printed data labels, 2, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 7, 18 and 22 deaths a year. The text calls these unexplained deaths in which ketamine was mentioned, low but increased 10-fold over the period; in most of them other psychotropic drugs were mentioned too, toxicology screens are done in about two-thirds of cases and ketamine is not tested routinely.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1; Physical and psychological harms › Acute physical risks › Risk of death from an acute dose, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: from 2 (1999) to 22 (2008) is an 11-fold rise; 62 mentions over the 10 years. The counts are deaths with ketamine mentioned, not deaths attributed to ketamine.

key_findings.finding: Accidents: two of 30 people who used ketamine frequently in the authors' 1-year longitudinal study (Morgan et al., ref. 31) died between baseline testing and the 12-month follow-up, which the review attributes to their acute ketamine use (one drowned in a bath, one died of hypothermia). Jansen and Stewart concluded that accidental death while intoxicated is the highest mortality risk, but the review says scientific data on accidental injury are sparse; in an interview study of 90 people who used ketamine (Muetzelfeldt et al., ref. 35), 13% reported having been in an accident as a direct result of taking ketamine and 83% knew someone who had.
key_findings.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Acute physical risks › Acute physical risk of death from accidents, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: How the two deaths were attributed to acute intoxication is not described.

key_findings.finding: TOXBASE, the UK National Poisons Unit's poisons information website for doctors: of 570 000 hits in 2008/09, 0.3% (1710) were ketamine-related, which the review calls a sixfold increase from 2000 (0.05%; 285 cases). No source is cited for these figures.
key_findings.locator: Acute ketamine poisoning and ER admissions, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The review calls the hits 'cases'; they are accesses to an information service, not patients. See reporting issues for the denominator.

key_findings.finding: Emergency presentations: at a London teaching hospital (Wood et al., ref. 36), 116 presentations involved recreational ketamine use, 11% with ketamine alone; co-ingested drugs included ethanol (39%), GHB/GBL (47%), cocaine (19%) and MDMA (53%); 72% were discharged directly from the emergency department, and no case with ketamine alone needed admission to critical care. In Hong Kong (Ng et al., ref. 37), 233 presentations: average age 22 years, two-thirds male; commonest presenting problems impaired consciousness (45%), abdominal pain (21%), lower urinary tract symptoms (12%) and dizziness (12%); signs reported as helping to identify intoxication were high blood pressure (40%), tachycardia (39%), abdominal tenderness (18%) and white powder in the nostrils (17%). The review reads the Hong Kong series as showing a lack of severe acute physical consequences.
key_findings.locator: Acute ketamine poisoning and ER admissions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Denominators of the co-ingestant percentages are not stated; whether 'average' is a mean or a median is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Acute cardiovascular effects, stated without any reference: ketamine raises heart rate, cardiac output and blood pressure, so it may pose an acute risk to people with hypertension or severe cardiac disease, those at risk of stroke and those with raised intracranial pressure; the review adds that acute cardiac risk is greater when ketamine is taken with stimulant drugs.
key_findings.locator: Acute physical risks › Acute cardiac risks from ketamine use (p. 30, continuing on p. 31)

key_findings.finding: Ulcerative cystitis, case evidence: Shahani et al. (ref. 38) first described nine people dependent on ketamine with urinary frequency and urgency, dysuria, urge incontinence and sometimes painful haematuria; CT showed marked bladder-wall thickening, small bladder capacity and perivesical stranding; all had severe ulcerative cystitis at cystoscopy; biopsies in four showed denuded urothelium with ulceration, granulation tissue and inflammatory cells; stopping ketamine gave some relief. Later case reports all describe people dependent on ketamine or using it near-daily. Oxley et al. (ref. 41) studied the histopathology of 17 people; the review says the lesions mimic carcinoma in situ and could raise the risk of bladder cancer. In Chu et al. (ref. 42), 42 of 59 patients (71%) had cystoscopic epithelial inflammation like that of chronic interstitial cystitis, detrusor overactivity or reduced bladder compliance (with or without vesico-ureteric reflux) was found in 47, and eight had raised serum creatinine.
key_findings.locator: Chronic physical and psychological effects of ketamine › Ketamine-induced ulcerative cystitis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Case series without comparison groups or denominators. No cancer incidence data are given; a raised cancer risk goes beyond histological mimicry, which is what the title of ref. 41 describes.

key_findings.finding: Prevalence, course and cause of cystitis: prevalence data are said to be difficult to obtain; of 90 people in the UK who used ketamine (Muetzelfeldt et al., ref. 35), 30% reported urinary tract symptoms while using it, and nearly half of those using frequently had sought medical attention for cystitis. According to Cottrell and Gillatt (ref. 43), about one-third of cases resolve after stopping ketamine, one-third stay the same and one-third worsen. The cause is unclear; the condition appears most common with frequent, mainly daily, use over an extended period, and the authors found only one case during medical use (a 16-year-old treated for chronic pain, whose symptoms remitted completely after her dose was reduced; ref. 40).
key_findings.locator: Ketamine-induced ulcerative cystitis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The one-third split comes from a one-page article in Practitioner (ref. 43) and the medical-use case from a letter to the editor (ref. 40); the 'nearly half' figure has no separate citation.

key_findings.finding: Kidney: in Chu et al. (ref. 42), 30 of 59 patients (51%) had hydronephrosis, unilateral in 7% and bilateral in 44%; four had papillary necrosis at the initial assessment, which led to renal failure in one, who had complete obstruction of the urethra. The review describes hydronephrosis secondary to urinary tract problems as an emerging problem with frequent, high-dose use.
key_findings.locator: Kidney dysfunction
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 4/59 = 6.8% and 26/59 = 44.1%, together 30 (50.8%); consistent.

key_findings.finding: Abdominal pain ('K-cramps') and the bile ducts: a third of the 90 people interviewed (ref. 35) spontaneously reported intense abdominal pain attributed to prolonged heavy use, and people using frequently often report taking more ketamine to relieve it, which can make attempts to stop fail. Three small case reports (one, three and two patients; refs 44–46) described colicky upper gastric pain in young people who used ketamine, all with abnormal liver function and CT dilatation of the common bile duct with a smooth tapered end mimicking choledochal cysts; the symptoms abated when ketamine was stopped. A larger emergency series, cited as ref. 46, is said to report abdominal pain in 21% and abnormal liver function in 15%.
key_findings.locator: 'K-cramps', 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref. 46 is cited both as one of the three case reports and as the larger series; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Depression in people who use ketamine: in the authors' 1-year longitudinal study (ref. 31), Beck Depression Inventory scores rose over the year in the daily-use and ex-use groups but not in people currently using infrequently (more than once a month, fewer than 3 times a week); the raised scores were not at clinical levels and the increase did not correlate with changes in ketamine use.
key_findings.locator: Depression, 1st paragraph (p. 31, continuing on p. 32)
key_findings.note: Neither statement is in the primary paper: Morgan et al. (2010b) reports the rise in depression scores (p. 128) and discusses it (p. 131) without describing the scores against clinical levels, and the only correlations with change in ketamine use it reports are for two cognitive tasks (p. 129) (reporting issue 16).

key_findings.finding: Antidepressant effects in patients, as summarized: a preliminary study of seven patients (Berman et al., ref. 47) suggested rapid and relatively prolonged effects of one dose in depression that had not responded to usual treatments. In Zarate et al. (ref. 48), 18 patients with treatment-resistant depression were given 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes; 12 showed an immediate 50% reduction in depression measures, against none of 14 patients given placebo; the effect of one dose lasted 1–2 weeks in eight patients, and the review says they all relapsed afterwards. In Aan het Rot et al. (ref. 49), patients received six infusions (days 0, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 12) depending on their response to the first; of nine who received repeated infusions, eight relapsed, within an estimated mean of 30 days after the first infusion or 19 days after the sixth. The review contrasts this speed with the 3–4-week lag of standard antidepressants and says chronic effects should be monitored if repeated dosing is to be used.
key_findings.locator: Depression, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The review does not say whether the 18 and the 14 were separate groups or the same patients; cite the primary trials (Berman et al., ref. 47, and Zarate et al., ref. 48, are on the project's Tier A list). See reporting issues for the day arithmetic.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis-like effects of single doses: in healthy volunteers, one dose of ketamine induces transient positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia (e.g. Krystal et al., ref. 50); in people with schizophrenia stabilized on antipsychotic medication, ketamine brings a resurgence of psychotic symptoms (Lahti et al., ref. 51), described as remarkably similar to each person's symptoms in the acute phase of the illness (Malhotra et al., ref. 52). In rats, about five repeated doses produced schizophrenia-like changes: abnormal hippocampal neurogenesis with fewer parvalbumin-containing GABAergic interneurons (ref. 53), and increased hippocampal dopamine binding with decreased prefrontal glutamate binding (ref. 54).
key_findings.locator: Psychosis, 1st paragraph and 2nd paragraph (first sentence)
key_findings.note: No doses, routes, rating scales or effect sizes are given for the human studies; cite the primary laboratory studies. By its title, ref. 52 studied patients free of neuroleptics, not patients stabilized on them.

key_findings.finding: Psychotic-like experiences in people who use ketamine: scores on measures of delusions, dissociation and schizotypy were higher with daily than with infrequent use, and with infrequent use than in polydrug controls who did not use ketamine (refs 31 and 55, both the authors' studies); the daily-use group showed a pattern of 'basic symptoms' similar to that of people in the prodrome of schizophrenia (ref. 31). The review says there is no evidence of clinical psychotic symptoms with infrequent use (ref. 56) and, despite anecdotes, little evidence of a link between chronic heavy use and a diagnosed psychotic disorder.
key_findings.locator: Psychosis, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The measures are not named and no scores are given; whether participants were intoxicated at testing is not stated. Of the two studies cited, the 1-year study (ref. 31; Morgan et al., 2010b, p. 128) reports the infrequent group above the non-drug controls only, not above the polydrug controls, and reports no test of daily against infrequent use on these scales; ref. 55 (Curran & Morgan, 2000, pp. 579–581) compared a ketamine group using ketamine from twice a week to once a month with polydrug controls on ratings of how people felt at that moment, taken 3 days after a night of use, not on everyday levels (reporting issue 16).

key_findings.finding: Acute effects on memory: the review states that in humans a single dose induces marked, dose-dependent impairments of working and episodic memory, citing the authors' own review (ref. 57), and that these would profoundly affect the ability to function; in mice, impaired fear memory was found after 4 but not 2 weeks of daily injections of 5 mg/kg (Amann et al., ref. 58).
key_findings.locator: Cognitive impairment, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No human study, dose, route, test or effect size is given; the statement about functioning is the authors' inference. For this round's controlled studies, cite the primary laboratory papers.

key_findings.finding: Lasting cognitive effects: infrequent or recreational use does not appear to be associated with long-term cognitive impairment (e.g. ref. 56); the review calls profound short- and long-term memory impairment in people using frequently the most robust finding (citing its authors' review, ref. 57). Many studies were cross-sectional and cannot address causation; the review states that in a longitudinal study frequent use “caused” impairments of visual recognition and spatial working memory that correlated with changes in use over 12 months (cited as ref. 30). Planning and other frontal impairments appear unrelated to measures of use (ref. 11). Memory impairments were not found in a group of 30 people who had been abstinent at least a year (no reference given), which the review takes as a sign that they may be reversible.
key_findings.locator: Cognitive impairment, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No tests, sample sizes (other than the 30), effect sizes or comparison groups are given. Ref. 30 is not the longitudinal study, which is ref. 31 (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran); see reporting issues. The 30 people abstinent at least a year cannot be matched to a primary report read here: the ex-ketamine group of 30 in Morgan et al. (2009) had been abstinent 120 to 2980 days (mean 344), so at least a year does not hold for it (reporting issue 16).

key_findings.finding: Brain imaging: increased D1 receptor binding in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of people who use ketamine (Narendran et al., ref. 56); white-matter abnormalities in people described as dependent on ketamine compared with controls (Liao et al., ref. 63), with reduced fractional anisotropy correlating with the degree of use in bilateral frontal and left temporoparietal regions, and small temporal changes that the review links tentatively to episodic memory. The review notes that similar changes have been seen in other drug-dependent populations (ref. 64), so they may not be specific to ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Neurological changes
key_findings.note: By its title, ref. 64 is a review of a common molecular pathway for addiction, not an imaging study.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacology as stated: ketamine is a non-competitive NMDA-receptor antagonist; it also blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, may potentiate GABA inhibition, induces dopamine release (ref. 1) and is a weak μ-opioid agonist (ref. 2); the S-(+) enantiomer is the more potent at the NMDA receptor and the two enantiomers have similar pharmacokinetic profiles (no reference). Ketamine raises extracellular dopamine in rat striatum and prefrontal cortex (ref. 66), and the review says some PET studies in humans show that it elicits striatal dopamine release (refs 67–69); its affinity for μ-opioid and σ sites is relatively low; S-ketamine has much greater NMDA affinity and R-ketamine greater opioid action (no reference).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (pp. 27–28); Dependence-related harms › Acute pleasure associated with taking the drug › Neurochemical actions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 33)
key_findings.note: By their titles, refs 67 and 69 are studies of prefrontal activation and of glucose metabolism; ref. 69 is held in this project as vollenweider_1997b. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Route and kinetics as stated, with no pharmacokinetic study cited: intranasal use is the commonest recreational route; intravenous use is rare in the United States even among people who inject other drugs (ref. 70); onset after insufflation is relatively rapid (about 5 minutes) and the half-life short (1–2 hours), which the review suggests may promote bingeing and add to ketamine's appeal over longer-acting hallucinogens (ref. 71, a qualitative study). Oral use is said to be rare because ketamine taken by mouth is quickly metabolized to norketamine (the review also characterizes the subjective effects by route, without a reference); intramuscular and occasional intravenous injection are mentioned.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Non-medical use of ketamine, 2nd paragraph (p. 28); Dependence-related harms › Pharmacokinetic parameters and route of administration (p. 33)
key_findings.note: None of these figures is sourced to a pharmacokinetic study; for kinetics by route cite the primary studies (clements_1982, yanagihara_2003) or peltoniemi_2016.

key_findings.finding: Reinforcing effects: in animals, self-administration of ketamine by rats (refs 72 and 73), conditioned place preference (ref. 74) and locomotor sensitization after repeated doses (refs 75–77) are reported, and ketamine substitutes for ethanol in drug-discrimination tests (refs 78 and 79); in recently detoxified people with alcohol dependence it produced ethanol-like subjective effects including a 'high' (Krystal et al., ref. 81), and in healthy volunteers it increases ratings of 'high' (ref. 82). In the authors' study (Morgan et al., ref. 83), healthy ketamine-naive volunteers received 0.4 or 0.8 mg/kg or placebo by intravenous infusion and rated how much they liked the drug and wanted more: shortly after the start both doses were liked and wanted; towards the end of the 80-minute infusion the ratings had fallen markedly in the high-dose group while the low-dose group still liked and wanted more, which the review calls an inverted U-shaped dose–response curve.
key_findings.locator: Acute reinforcing effects in animals and humans, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ratings were taken during the infusion. The review describes separate dose groups but gives no group sizes, statistics, order or blinding. Several animal references do not match their sentence by title; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Dependence: case reports exist (refs 84–87) but there are no large-scale studies, so the incidence of ketamine dependence is unknown. In the interview study of 90 people (Muetzelfeldt et al., ref. 35), concern about addiction to ketamine was expressed by 57% of those using frequently, 43% of those using infrequently and 60% of those who had stopped; most of those using frequently reported using without stopping until supplies ran out.
key_findings.locator: Psychological and physical dependence › Incidence of ketamine dependence

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal and craving: the evidence on a withdrawal syndrome is called conflicting. In a study of 30 people using ketamine daily (Morgan et al., ref. 88), 28 had tried and failed to stop, all citing craving as the reason, and 12 reported withdrawal symptoms on stopping (anxiety, shaking, sweating, palpitations); a few case reports describe craving and anxiety; a specific withdrawal syndrome had not been described.
key_findings.locator: Psychological and physical dependence › Withdrawal symptoms following abstinence
key_findings.note: Self-report in one group of 30; no instrument or comparison group is described.

key_findings.finding: Tolerance: studies in rats (ref. 92), monkeys (ref. 93) and children undergoing anaesthesia (e.g. ref. 94) are said to have “convincingly demonstrated” rapid tolerance with repeated dosing, possibly through induction of liver enzymes (ref. 95) or adaptation of receptor number or sensitivity. People using frequently report escalating amounts, one study finding a 600% increase from first to current use (ref. 88, self-report); in the authors' longitudinal study (ref. 31), hair ketamine concentrations doubled over a year in people using infrequently and did not change in people using frequently, who the review says were probably already using maximal amounts.
key_findings.locator: Psychological and physical dependence › Tolerance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: By its title, ref. 94 is a case report of one infant; refs 92 and 93 are from the 1970s and 1960s (reference list). A rise in hair concentration shows more use, whether from tolerance or from more frequent use, and the explanation for the unchanged values is not supported by data in the review.

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor performance and risk: ketamine impairs psychomotor performance dose-dependently, such as hand–eye coordination and balance (Lofwall et al., ref. 96, by its title a study of intramuscular ketamine in healthy adults), which the review links to accident risk in complex tasks such as driving; over a 4-year period, 21% of fatal vehicle crashes in Hong Kong involved alcohol or drugs and 9% of those involved ketamine (ref. 97); people with more dependent use report using in most situations, including while driving (ref. 35). Ketamine use is associated with more unsafe sex among gay men in the United States (e.g. ref. 98); the review states, citing the Advisory Council's technical committee report (ref. 21), that ketamine is not associated with violent behaviour.
key_findings.locator: Social harms of ketamine › Social harms of intoxication › Risk of accidental injury; Risk-taking behaviour
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 9% of 21% is about 1.9% of fatal crashes, and involvement is not causation. No data are given for the statement on violence.

key_findings.finding: Education and work: the review states that there are no data on how ketamine dependence affects achievement; people with dependent use in the UK are often part of subcultures (traveller and free-party scenes) whose educational and professional achievement may have differed from the norm irrespective of ketamine (refs 99 and 100); 20% of 100 people interviewed (Dillon et al., ref. 101) perceived employment-related problems from their ketamine use; and in the authors' study (Morgan et al., ref. 31) the frequent or daily-use group had spent significantly fewer years in education than the infrequent-use and non-using groups.
key_findings.locator: Social harms of ketamine › Educational and professional achievement
key_findings.note: Fewer years of education in the frequent-use group is also a confounder for the cognitive comparisons from the same study, which the review's section on cognitive impairment does not discuss.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy: no data on ketamine use in human pregnancy were available; in rodents, cocaine and cocaine combined with ketamine reduced fetal birth weight, but ketamine alone did not (ref. 103).
key_findings.locator: Social harms of ketamine › Ketamine use in pregnancy
key_findings.note: The text says rats; the title of ref. 103 names CF-1 mice (p. 38).

key_findings.finding: Prevalence and market, as cited: British Crime Survey estimates of the number of people using ketamine rose from about 85 000 in 2006/07 to 113 000 in 2008/09; past-year use among 16–24-year-olds was 0.9% in 2007/08, 1.9% in 2008/09 and 1.7% in 2009/10 (against 2009/10 figures of 16.1% for cannabis, 5.5% cocaine, 4.3% ecstasy, 3.2% 'amyl nitrate' as printed, 2.4% amphetamines and 1.2% magic mushrooms), and lifetime use in this age group 2.2%, 3.6% and 4% over the same three years; in the United States an estimated 1–2% of 10th and 12th graders had ever used ketamine. Ketamine became a Class C drug in the UK in 2006, and the average UK price of a gram fell from £30 to £20 between 2005 and 2008. Among clubbers, 25% had taken ketamine in a 2001 survey and 68% in a 2009 survey, in which a third of respondents reported use in the previous month, which the review reads as making ketamine the fourth most popular drug among UK clubbers. There were 1266 ketamine seizures in the UK in 2008/09.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Non-medical use of ketamine, 4th paragraph (pp. 28–29) and 5th paragraph (p. 29); Social harms of ketamine › Engagement in criminal activities (p. 34)
key_findings.note: Second-hand survey figures; the 2001 and 2009 clubber figures come from different surveys (refs 19 and 20, the second published in a magazine) and are not a trend in one population. For prevalence claims, cite the surveys themselves.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: ulcerative cystitis is the harm of most concern, appearing more common in, but not restricted to, frequent and often daily use; its mechanism and why only some people develop it are named as key research questions; dependence is a concern although its incidence is hard to gauge, and tolerance is said to develop rapidly; urological and psychosocial treatment should be coordinated; and long-term neurological, cognitive and psychiatric effects need longitudinal studies that also follow people who stop. The authors judge that the UK Class C classification does not accurately reflect ketamine's known and potentially severe harms, while noting little evidence that changing a drug's legal class changes behaviour (since classification, prevalence rose and price fell) and that a stricter class would hinder legitimate medical use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 34) and 4th to 6th paragraphs (p. 35)

reporting_issues.issue: The methods are presented as systematic but cannot be reproduced: the abstract says the literature was “systematically searched” and the methods mention pre-specified criteria and a design hierarchy, but no search strings, criteria, counts of records screened or included, list of included studies or evidence level for any study are given. The cut-off is given as an initial review to September 2010, yet the list includes a 2011 paper (ref. 80) and web sources accessed on 19 July 2011 (refs 14 and 21).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be treated as systematic and its effective search date is unclear; the absence of a study from it says nothing about whether that study existed.

reporting_issues.issue: One of the nine categories of the stated framework, propensity for intravenous use, has no section of its own (intravenous use appears in one sentence each on pp. 28 and 33), and no category is scored.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for an ISCD harm rating of ketamine or for its propensity for intravenous use.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence stating that no adverse outcomes are reported even after marked overdose in medical settings cites ref. 27, which the reference list gives as a report of a ketamine medication error resulting in death.
reporting_issues.consequence: The categorical safety statement is contradicted by its own citation; a claim about large doses in medical settings must go to the primary reports (ref. 27; Green et al., 1999), not to this sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Safety ratio: it is defined as the ratio of a usual recreational dose to a lethal dose, the inverse of the way the value of 25 is built (lethal estimate over usual dose); the two figures printed for the calculation give 24, not 25 (editors' calculation); the lower mouse figure of 42.9 mg/kg has no route stated and comes from a study whose title concerns midazolam's effect on lethality; and the ratio is for oral use, which the review describes as rare (p. 28).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the ratio only as Gable's extrapolation from rodent oral data; it is not a measured human margin and does not apply to the routes the review describes as common.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 and its text describe the same counts differently: the caption calls them post-mortem toxicology mentions of ketamine, the text unexplained deaths in which ketamine was mentioned, most also involving other psychotropic drugs. The text's 10-fold increase is 11-fold on the printed labels (2 in 1999, 22 in 2008; editors' calculation). Part of the series comes from additional data supplied by J. Corkery, since ref. 105 covers 1993–2006.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe these as deaths in which ketamine was detected or mentioned, not deaths caused by ketamine, and should note that the 2007 and 2008 counts have no published source in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: TOXBASE: no source is given, and the 2000 count of 285 at 0.05% implies the same denominator of 570 000 hits as in 2008/09 (editors' calculation: 285 / 0.0005 = 570 000).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the service had the same number of hits in both years or the 2000 count was derived from the later total; the 'sixfold increase' in cases is then the rise in share by construction, and hits on an information service are not patients.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 46 is cited for two different things on the same page: as one of three small case reports (two patients) of dilated bile ducts, and as a larger study of emergency presentations with abdominal pain in 21% and abnormal liver function in 15%. The reference list gives ref. 46 as a one-page item with an author reply, and the 21% matches the abdominal-pain figure given for the 233 Hong Kong presentations of Ng et al. (ref. 37) on p. 30. By its title, ref. 45, also counted among the three bile-duct case reports, concerns obstructive nephropathy and kidney injury.
reporting_issues.consequence: The larger series is probably ref. 37, but the 15% liver-function figure cannot be traced to a source, and it is uncertain that all three case reports describe bile-duct findings; read refs 37 and 44–46 before citing.

reporting_issues.issue: The longitudinal memory finding is cited to ref. 30, a 2001 article on ketamine as a street drug in an emergency-services journal; the 1-year longitudinal study is ref. 31 (Morgan et al., 2010). The same sentence uses a causal verb for a correlation over 12 months in an observational study.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about memory change with continued use must cite Morgan et al. (2010) directly and describe an association; this sentence cannot carry a causal claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no reference: the TOXBASE figures (p. 30); the whole cardiac paragraph (pp. 30–31); the absence of memory impairment in 30 people abstinent at least a year (p. 32); the onset time and half-life in the pharmacokinetics paragraph, whose only references are a study of ketamine use among young people who inject drugs and a qualitative study (p. 33); and the statement that nearly half of those using frequently had sought medical attention for cystitis (p. 31).
reporting_issues.consequence: These cannot be checked from the review; claims need primary sources (for kinetics, the pharmacokinetic studies on this round's list).

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that PET studies in humans show striatal dopamine release cites refs 67–69, but by their titles ref. 67 (Breier et al., 1997) concerns focal activation of the prefrontal cortex and ref. 69 (Vollenweider et al., 1997, held in this project as vollenweider_1997b) is an [18F]FDG glucose-metabolism study; only ref. 68 (Smith et al., 1998) is titled as a [11C]raclopride study of dopamine. The introduction cites ref. 1 for dopamine release, a paper whose title asks whether striatal dopamine release elicited by NMDA antagonists can be seen by imaging at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: The human dopamine-release statement rests on at most one of the three cited PET studies; vollenweider_1997b must not be cited for striatal dopamine release on this review's authority, and the doubt signalled by the title of ref. 1 is not discussed.

reporting_issues.issue: Animal statements whose references do not match by title: self-administration of ketamine by rats cites ref. 73, titled as a study of phencyclidine self-administration by rats; conditioned place preference cites ref. 74, titled as a study of ketamine's effect on morphine-induced place preference in mice; ethanol substitution in rats cites ref. 78, titled as a study in mice; and the pregnancy statement about rats cites ref. 103, titled as a study in CF-1 mice.
reporting_issues.consequence: The preclinical summaries cannot be cited without the primary papers; the pregnancy result comes from mice.

reporting_issues.issue: Other citations that by their titles do not fit the sentence: refs 10 and 11, given as examples of single-dose experimental studies of the ketamine model of psychosis (p. 28), are a review of overlapping memory deficits and the authors' comparison of frequent, infrequent and former use; ref. 52, cited for the resemblance to each patient's acute illness in people stabilized on antipsychotics, describes patients free of neuroleptics; ref. 64, cited for white-matter changes in other drug-dependent populations, is a review of molecular pathways in addiction; ref. 33, a 1978 book that the review also cites as an anecdotal source (p. 30), is the only support for different neurochemical properties of the isomers (p. 33); ref. 94, cited for children under anaesthesia as part of convincingly demonstrated tolerance, is a case report of one infant; and ref. 39, cited as a case report of cystitis, carries the same title as ref. 42 with an author reply, so it appears to be a letter on that paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements resting on these references have weaker or different support than the text implies; claims should not repeat them without the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Depression paragraph: with the sixth infusion on day 12, a mean of 30 days after the first infusion is 18 days, not 19, after the sixth (editors' calculation); the 2010 repeated-infusion study is called the first clinical trial although the same paragraph describes the 2006 study whose title calls it a randomized trial (ref. 48); and it is not said whether the 18 patients given ketamine and the 14 given placebo were separate groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the trial figures should be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Abstract against body: the abstract concludes that neurocognitive impairment in frequent use can harm achievement in education and at work and compound addiction problems, but the body states that there are no data on how ketamine dependence affects achievement and that the subcultures concerned may differ in achievement irrespective of ketamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: The educational and occupational consequence is the authors' inference, not a finding; no claim may cite this review as evidence for it.

reporting_issues.issue: Groups of 30 recur: 30 people using frequently in the 1-year longitudinal study (ref. 31, p. 30), 30 using daily in the craving and withdrawal study (ref. 88, p. 33) and 30 people abstinent at least a year (no reference, p. 32), the first two from the authors' own studies; the review does not say whether these groups overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: Findings from these groups should not be counted as independent replications unless the primary papers show the samples are distinct.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors: 'optimal isomers' for the two enantiomers (p. 27), 'amyl nitrate' among the comparison drugs (p. 29), 'reduction of her of ketamine dose' (p. 31), and the author of ref. 102 printed as 'Bulletin H. O. S.' (p. 38).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the figures; take care when quoting the wording.

reporting_issues.issue: Four statements about the authors' own studies differ from the primary papers read for this round: (1) the 1-year rise in depression scores is said to be below clinical levels and unrelated to changes in ketamine use (pp. 31–32), which Morgan et al. (2010b) does not report; (2) 30 people abstinent at least a year are said to show no memory impairment (p. 32, no reference), whereas the ex-ketamine group of 30 in Morgan et al. (2009) had been abstinent 120 to 2980 days; (3) infrequent use is said to score above polydrug controls on delusions, dissociation and schizotypy, citing refs 31 and 55 (p. 32), but ref. 31 reports this against non-drug controls only and ref. 55 used ratings of how people felt at that moment, 3 days after a night of use; (4) infrequent use is defined as more than once a month and fewer than 3 times a week (pp. 31, 32), where the primary papers define it as less than four times a week but at least once a month.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements should be cited from the primary papers, with their own figures, definitions and comparison groups, not from the review.

disagreements.first_pass: No tests, sample sizes (other than the 30), effect sizes or comparison groups are given. Ref. 30 is not the longitudinal study, which is ref. 31 (Morgan, Muetzelfeldt and Curran); see reporting issues.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: the review describes the 30 people who had stopped as abstinent for at least a year (p. 32, no reference), which conflicts with the primary figures for Morgan et al. (2009): a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980; key finding 18 and the interpretation gap repeat the year without flagging the conflict.
disagreements.resolution: Verified: review p. 32 (Cognitive impairment, 2nd paragraph) and Morgan et al. (2009), Table 2 (p. 81). Note extended; reporting issue 16 added. The interpretation gap is flagged at the same point (entry for interpretation_gap.results_show).

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: the review's definition of infrequent use (more than once a month, under 3 times a week; pp. 31, 32) differs from the claims' description of the Morgan et al. (2009) infrequent group (at least monthly, less than four times a week); one of the two is wrong; check against morgan_2009.
disagreements.resolution: Checked: Morgan et al. (2009, p. 78) and Morgan et al. (2010b, p. 122) both define infrequent use as less than four times a week but at least once a month; the review's definition differs from its own primary studies. Note added; included in reporting issue 16.

disagreements.first_pass: The measures are not named and no scores are given; whether participants were intoxicated at testing is not stated.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: ref. 55 (Curran & Morgan, 2000), cited for people using infrequently scoring above polydrug controls on delusions, dissociation and schizotypy, measured state ratings 3 days after a night of use in a group using twice a week to monthly, so the review mixes residual state effects with everyday levels. Also the claim writer's report (AI reader 202): the 2009 and 2010 papers report infrequent use above non-drug controls only.
disagreements.resolution: Verified: review p. 32 (Psychosis, 2nd paragraph); Morgan et al. (2010b), p. 128 (infrequent group above the non-drug group only; no frequent-against-infrequent test); Morgan et al. (2009), p. 83 (infrequent above non-drug); Curran & Morgan (2000), pp. 579–581 (state scales, day-3 ratings). Note extended; included in reporting issue 16.

disagreements.reviewer: Claim writer's report (AI reader 202), card findings: the review says the one-year rise in depression was not clinical and was unrelated to change in use; Morgan et al. (2010b) says neither.
disagreements.resolution: Verified in Morgan et al. (2010b): the BDI results (p. 128), the correlations (p. 129) and the Discussion of depression (p. 131) contain neither statement. Note added; included in reporting issue 16.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227 (missed items above) and the claim writer's report (AI reader 202): the review's statements on the depression rise, the 30 abstinent people and infrequent use against polydrug controls go beyond the primary papers.
disagreements.resolution: Each checked against the primary PDFs (Morgan et al., 2009, pp. 78, 81, 83; Morgan et al., 2010b, pp. 122, 128–131; Curran & Morgan, 2000, pp. 579–581). Collected in one reporting issue so that the key findings' notes can point to it.

disagreements.first_pass: ... not found with infrequent use or in 30 people abstinent for a year; ...
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 227, missed: key finding 18 and the interpretation gap repeat the year of abstinence without flagging its conflict with the primary figures.
disagreements.resolution: Factual flag added beside the review's statement (Morgan et al., 2009, Table 2, p. 81: 120 to 2980 days); the rating (substantial) is unchanged.
